title: Greater love (John 15:13)
hookLine: greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends

lines: FIRST SAID AT A SUPPER TABLE.
cards: Greater love than this no man hath. The sentence has been carved in stone on war memorials, set on plaques for firefighters, read aloud in eulogies for nurses and soldiers.
People reach for it when someone has given everything for someone else. Usually it stands alone, with no chapter around it, as if it were written for a monument.
It was actually said at a supper table, the night before the one who said it died.

teach.h: AS I HAVE LOVED YOU, MEANS THIS.
teach.b: Jesus has just repeated his commandment: love one another as I have loved you. Then he shows what as I have loved you is going to mean.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." The Greek for life here is psychē, the word that also means soul, the whole self.

teach.h: LAY DOWN: THE TOWEL, THE CROSS.
teach.b: And lay down is the same verb Jesus used about the good shepherd: I lay down my life for my sheep. It echoes the supper itself, too.
In chapter thirteen he laid down his garments to wash their feet, and took them up again. Lay down, take up. The towel and the cross are drawn in the same strokes.
He's not describing a hero somewhere else. He's describing tomorrow afternoon. Catholics have a modern face for this verse.
At Auschwitz, after a prisoner escaped, the guards chose men to starve to death in a bunker. One of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and children.
A Franciscan priest, Maximilian Kolbe, stepped forward and asked to take his place.

teach.h: A LIFE LAID DOWN A LITTLE AT A TIME.
teach.b: He was allowed to, and he died in that bunker.
Gajowniczek survived the war and lived to see Pope John Paul the Second declare Kolbe a saint. But the verse isn't only about dying.
A parent's sleep given up for years, a caregiver's evenings, a career paused for a sick friend: some readers see those too as a life laid down a little at a time.

how: The Church keeps a yearly memorial of Saint Maximilian Kolbe, and John 15:13 is often read at the funerals of people who died serving others.

o: giving your very life for your friends

games.q: you're a prisoner standing in a line at Auschwitz. men are being chosen to die, and one of them cries out for his family. what does Maximilian Kolbe do?
o: steps forward and asks to take his place.
games.why: Kolbe, a Franciscan priest, asked to die in the man's place. he was allowed to, and died in the bunker.

practice: Bring one friend to mind, someone who could use a hand right now, and look at your own day for something to set down for them: an hour, a plan, a preference, the right to be right.
Let it be real but small, and picture handing it over. If you pray, hold the line, greater love than this no man hath; if you don't, just hold your friend's face.

wordCard.voice: Greater love. Jesus at the supper: no one has greater love than to lay down their life for their friends. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love, the word used in John 15:13 for greater love.

carryVoice: Your line: lay down your life. Love, measured the way he loved. See you tomorrow.
